title: CSC_106 — End of Semester Objective Exam

questions.q: According to the Week 1 material, the World Wide Web was introduced by:
options: Vinton Cerf in 1974
Sir Tim Berners-Lee in 1989
Sir Tim Berners-Lee in 1991
Robert Kahn in 1969
questions.why: — **[no deck]** (Week 1's deck is "Introduction to Web Development"; the history is Summary-only) Why B is right: the Week 1 Summary states "In 1989, Sir Tim Berners-Lee introduced the World Wide Web". Why the others are wrong: A names a co-author of TCP/IP and the year of the TCP specification — Internet infrastructure, not the Web · C is the year most outside sources give for the first public web page, and it is the trap for anyone answering from general knowledge instead of the course · D pairs the other TCP/IP co-author with ARPANET's first message, conflating the Internet's origin with the Web's.

questions.q: The course describes ARPANET as a network that was:
options: built by CERN specifically to host the first web pages
commercial from the outset and later opened to universities
initially developed for military purposes and later expanded to academic use
designed for academic research and later taken over by the military
questions.why: — **[no deck]** Why C is right: the Summary's exact words are "The ARPANET, initially developed for military purposes, expanded to academic use." Why the others are wrong: A credits CERN, which is where Berners-Lee worked on the Web twenty years later, not where ARPANET began · B invents a commercial origin · D reverses the stated order, the single most common slip on this bullet.

questions.q: Which statement matches the distinction the Week 1 summary states twice?
options: The Internet is the infrastructure and the World Wide Web is an application built upon it
The World Wide Web is the infrastructure and the Internet is the traffic carried over it
The Internet and the World Wide Web are interchangeable names for the same system
The Internet is the set of hyperlinked documents; the Web is the cabling that carries them
questions.why: — **[no deck]** Why A is right: the Summary says it twice — "distinguish between the Internet as an infrastructure and the World Wide Web as an application". Why the others are wrong: B inverts infrastructure and application · C is the error the sheet explicitly names as the thing to avoid · D swaps the definitions, treating documents as the network and cabling as the Web.

questions.q: The deck states the browser–server interaction as a four-step sequence. Which order is correct?
options: URL entered → server processes the request → browser sends an HTTP request → browser renders
Browser sends an HTTP request → URL entered → server sends a response → browser renders
URL entered → browser renders the page → browser sends an HTTP request → server responds
URL entered → browser sends an HTTP request → server processes and responds → browser renders
questions.why: Why D is right: the deck's four steps are user enters a URL or clicks a link → browser sends an HTTP request → server processes it and returns an HTTP response → browser renders the content. Why the others are wrong: A has the server processing before a request has been sent · B starts with a request that no user action triggered · C renders before any content has arrived, the classic misreading of "the browser displays the page then fetches it".

questions.q: The deck names three key components of web browsers and servers. They are:
options: URL, DNS and TCP/IP
URL, HTTP and HTML/CSS/JavaScript
HTTP, FTP and SMTP
HTML, CSS and PHP
questions.why: Why B is right: the deck's "Key Components of Web Browsers and Servers" slide names exactly three — Uniform Resource Locator, Hypertext Transfer Protocol, and HTML/CSS/JavaScript. Why the others are wrong: A substitutes DNS and TCP/IP, which are real infrastructure but are not on that slide · C lists three transfer protocols from Week 2, a different lesson · D swaps in PHP, a Week 9 server-side language, for JavaScript.

questions.q: In the deck's four-way taxonomy of servers, Node.js is given as an example of a:
options: application server
web server
database server
proxy server
questions.why: Why A is right: the four server types are web, database, application and proxy; Node.js is the only example the deck gives for **application server**. Why the others are wrong: B is where a working developer files Node.js, since it serves HTTP — but the deck's web-server examples are Apache, Nginx and IIS · C is where MySQL, PostgreSQL and MongoDB sit · D has no named example at all in the deck.

questions.q: In the Week 1 classification of development tools, Visual Studio Code is listed as:
options: an integrated development environment, alongside WebStorm and Eclipse
a browser developer tool for inspecting and debugging pages
a text editor, alongside Sublime Text and Atom
a version control system, alongside Git and GitLab
questions.why: Why C is right: the deck puts Visual Studio Code under **text editors** with Sublime Text and Atom, and Microsoft Visual Studio (a different product) under IDEs. Why the others are wrong: A is correct by any working definition and wrong for this exam — the confusion between Visual Studio Code and Visual Studio is exactly what the question tests · B and D name the other two tool categories, browser developer tools and version control systems.

questions.q: The deck states three advantages of client–server architecture. They are:
options: scalability, low latency and cross-browser compatibility
centralised data management, fault tolerance and statelessness
separation of concerns, encryption and load balancing
scalability, centralised data management and separation of concerns
questions.why: Why D is right: the deck names three advantages and only three — scalability, centralised data management, separation of concerns. Why the others are wrong: A imports low latency from the WebSocket slide and cross-browser compatibility from jQuery · B adds fault tolerance (a Week 11 load-balancing benefit) and statelessness (a REST constraint) · C adds encryption and load balancing, which are server functions rather than advantages of the architecture. --- ### Week 2 — Protocols, markup languages, email, DNS

questions.q: The default port numbers for HTTP and HTTPS are:
questions.why: — **[no deck]** (no slide in the semester gives a port number) Why A is right: HTTP is port 80, HTTPS is port 443. Why the others are wrong: B gives 8080, the conventional *alternate* HTTP port used by development servers, not the default · C compounds that error · D reverses the pair, which is the answer of someone who has memorised the numbers but not which is which.

questions.q: HTTPS is best described as:
options: a protocol unrelated to HTTP that replaces it entirely
HTTP carried inside an SSL/TLS encrypted channel
HTTP with form data moved from the URL into the request body
HTTP running over UDP rather than over TCP
questions.why: — **[no deck]** (the Week 2 Summary gives four bullets; "SSL/TLS encryption" comes from the Week 11 Summary) Why B is right: HTTPS is HTTP carried inside a TLS tunnel — the same protocol, encrypted. Why the others are wrong: A treats HTTPS as a separate protocol, the commonest conceptual error · C describes the difference between GET and POST, not between HTTP and HTTPS · D describes HTTP/3 over QUIC, which is a real thing but not what HTTPS means.

questions.q: A logged-in user requests a page their account is not permitted to see. The server identifies them successfully but refuses to serve it. Which status code is correct?
options: 400 Bad Request
401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found
questions.why: — **[no deck]** Why C is right: 403 Forbidden is the server saying "I know who you are and you still may not have this." Why the others are wrong: A is for a malformed request the server cannot parse · B is the adjacent code and the trap: despite being spelled "Unauthorized", 401 means *unauthenticated* — no or bad credentials · D would deny the resource exists, which is sometimes used deliberately but is not what the question describes.

questions.q:
Consider the following request.
```http
GET /chat HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13
```
Which status line does the server return when it accepts this?
options: HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
questions.why: — **[no deck]** (WebSocket is in the deck; the handshake and its status code are not) Why A is right: the server completes a WebSocket upgrade with 101 Switching Protocols, after which the connection is no longer HTTP. Why the others are wrong: B would mean the server treated it as an ordinary GET and returned a body, i.e. the upgrade failed · C is for resource creation after a POST · D is a redirect and would abandon the handshake entirely.

questions.q:
Consider the following session transcript.
```
220 ftp.example.com FTP server ready
USER ade
331 Password required for ade
PASS secret123
230 User ade logged in
PASV
227 Entering Passive Mode (192,0,2,1,195,80)
RETR report.pdf
226 Transfer complete
```
What does this exchange demonstrate about the security weakness the course attributes to FTP?
options: Passive mode lets the server open the data connection back to the client
The RETR command transfers the file without any integrity check
Port 21 is being used for data rather than for control commands
The user's password crosses the network in plaintext
questions.why: — **[no deck]** (FTP has no lecture slides anywhere; the Week 2 Summary gives three bullets) Why D is right: `PASS secret123` travels in the clear. The course's phrase is that FTP "lacks encryption, making data vulnerable" — and it is the *credentials*, not only the file, that are exposed. Why the others are wrong: A describes active mode, not passive; this transcript shows PASV, where the client opens both connections · B is true but is not what the course means by vulnerable · C misreads the ports — 21 is the control channel, which is what this transcript shows, and the 227 reply is handing out a separate data port.

questions.q: Which statement about SFTP is accurate?
options: It is FTP with a TLS layer added, on port 21 or port 990
It runs over SSH on port 22 as a single encrypted connection
It uses two encrypted connections, on ports 20 and 21
It is a secure form of HTTP designed for large file transfers
questions.why: — **[no deck]** Why B is right: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol, a subsystem of SSH on port 22, one encrypted connection. Why the others are wrong: A describes **FTPS**, the protocol students most often confuse with SFTP — FTPS really is FTP with TLS bolted on · C keeps FTP's two-connection design, which SFTP does not share · D confuses it with HTTPS. Note the course calls SFTP "a secure extension of FTP"; write that phrase in a written paper, but know it shares no code, commands or port with FTP.

questions.q: Which pairing of markup language and primary use matches the deck?
options: SVG — representing mathematical notation and equations
XML — describing two-dimensional vector graphics
MathML — storing and exchanging structured data
XHTML — HTML reformulated as an XML application
questions.why: Why D is right: the deck says XHTML "reformulates HTML as an XML application". Why the others are wrong: A gives MathML's purpose to SVG · B gives SVG's purpose to XML · C gives XML's purpose to MathML. Each distractor is a real purpose from the same five-item list, attached to the wrong language — the standard way this list is examined.

questions.q:
Consider the following document.
```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<library>
  <book>
    <title>JavaScript: The Good Parts</title>
    <author>Douglas Crockford</author>
    <price>19.50</price>
  </book>
</library>
```
Which feature of XML, in the deck's own phrasing, does this illustrate?
options: It uses a fixed vocabulary of tags defined by specification
It defines the layout and presentation of the data in a browser
It employs a user-defined set of tags to describe data
It requires a stylesheet before any of its tags can be parsed
questions.why: Why C is right: `library`, `book`, `title`, `author` and `price` are invented by the document's author. The deck's discriminator is that XML "employs a user-defined set of tags to describe data". Why the others are wrong: A describes HTML, whose tag vocabulary is fixed by specification — this is the exact contrast the slide draws · B calls XML a presentation language, which it is not; XML says nothing about appearance · D confuses well-formedness with styling — an XML document parses without any stylesheet.

questions.q: According to the deck, SVG's principal advantage is that:
options: it compresses photographs to smaller files than PNG
graphics can be scaled without losing image quality
it renders faster because the browser skips the layout stage
it stores images as binary data that the browser decodes natively
questions.why: Why B is right: SVG describes graphics as shapes and coordinates, so they "can be scaled without losing image quality". Why the others are wrong: A is false for photographs, where raster formats win — vector markup suits logos, icons and diagrams · C invents a rendering shortcut · D describes a binary raster format; SVG is markup, which is why it appears in a markup-languages lecture at all.

questions.q:
Consider the following session transcript.
```
220 smtp.example.com ESMTP ready
HELO mail.miva.edu.ng
250 Hello mail.miva.edu.ng
MAIL FROM:<ade@miva.edu.ng>
250 Sender OK
RCPT TO:<lecturer@example.com>
250 Recipient OK
```
Which command identifies the intended recipient of the message?
options: RCPT TO
MAIL FROM
HELO
DATA
questions.why: Why A is right: `RCPT TO` names the recipient. The deck's ordered list is HELO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, then the message content. Why the others are wrong: B names the *sender*, and swapping the two is the single most common SMTP mistake · C is the greeting that opens the session and identifies the connecting host · D begins the message body and appears after all recipients are declared.

questions.q: A student wants their mail to remain on the server and stay in step across a phone and a laptop. Which protocol does the deck describe for this, and why?
options: POP3, because messages are downloaded to the device and removed from the server
SMTP, because it relays messages between servers across different domains
IMAP, because messages stay on the server and actions on one device appear on others
MIME, because it handles character encoding consistently across devices
questions.why: Why C is right: the deck's two IMAP key functions are email synchronisation ("actions taken on one device are reflected on others") and server-based storage. Why the others are wrong: A is POP3, and the reason given is precisely why it is wrong here — POP3 downloads and removes, so a second device finds nothing · B confuses sending with retrieval; SMTP never retrieves mail · D treats MIME as a protocol, when it is a standard governing message *format*.

questions.q: MIME is best described as:
options: a retrieval protocol that downloads attachments separately from the message
a standard that extends the email message format beyond plain ASCII text
a protocol that relays messages between mail servers across domains
a DNS record type identifying the mail servers for a domain
questions.why: Why B is right: MIME extends the message format to support non-ASCII character sets, attachments, and audio, video and images. Why the others are wrong: A makes MIME a retrieval protocol, confusing it with POP3/IMAP · C describes SMTP relaying · D describes the MX record, which is DNS and shares only the letter M.

questions.q:
Consider the domain name below.
```
admin.example.com
```
Reading it as the deck does, which statement is correct?
options: "admin" is the TLD, "example" a subdomain, "com" the second-level domain
"com" is the root domain, "example" the TLD, "admin" the second-level domain
"admin" is the second-level domain, "example" the TLD, "com" a subdomain
"com" is the TLD, "example" the second-level domain, "admin" a subdomain
questions.why: Why D is right: read a domain right to left. The deck's own worked illustration of `admin.example.com` gives com as the TLD, example as the second-level domain, admin as a subdomain. Why the others are wrong: A reads left to right, the error the deck's illustration exists to prevent · B promotes "com" to the root domain — the root is the unnamed level *above* all TLDs · C shuffles all three labels.

questions.q: DNSSEC protects the Domain Name System by:
options: adding digital signatures to DNS data to ensure integrity and authenticity
encrypting DNS queries so that they cannot be read in transit
routing queries through a proxy that conceals the client's IP address
restricting DNS responses to authoritative servers only
questions.why: Why A is right: the deck says DNSSEC "adds digital signatures to DNS data, ensuring data integrity and authenticity", and helps prevent cache poisoning by verifying response authenticity. Why the others are wrong: B is the most tempting wrong answer — DNSSEC **signs**, it does not **encrypt**; queries stay readable · C describes an anonymising proxy or DNS-over-HTTPS, neither of which is DNSSEC · D invents a restriction and drags in port 53, which no slide mentions.

questions.q: The deck describes REST as:
options: a protocol that replaces HTTP for building web services
an architectural style and set of constraints, stateless and resource-based
a message format built from XML envelopes and bodies
a full-duplex channel held open over a single TCP connection
questions.why: Why B is right: the slide calls REST "an architectural style and set of constraints for designing networked applications", stateless and resource-based. Why the others are wrong: A is what the deck's *heading* implies — it files REST under "Web Communication Protocols" and contradicts itself; the slide body is what to answer from · C describes SOAP's XML envelope · D describes WebSocket. Every distractor here is a neighbouring item from the same three-protocol lesson. --- ### Week 3 — HTML structure, hyperlinks and forms

questions.q: The four key components of an HTML document, as the deck lists them, are:
options: `<html>`, `<head>`, `<title>`, `<body>`
`<!DOCTYPE>`, `<meta>`, `<head>`, `<body>`
`<!DOCTYPE>`, `<html>`, `<head>`, `<body>`
`<html>`, `<header>`, `<main>`, `<footer>`
questions.why: Why C is right: the deck's four named components are the Document Type Declaration, the `<html>` root element, the head section and the body section. Why the others are wrong: A drops the DOCTYPE, which the deck calls "the very first line", and promotes `<title>`, a child of `<head>` · B replaces `<html>` with `<meta>`, another head child · D lists semantic sectioning elements, which belong to a different slide entirely.

questions.q: According to the deck, the `<head>` section:
options: holds meta-information and is not visible to the user
holds the visible content, including headings and paragraphs
is optional whenever no external stylesheet is linked
must appear after `<body>` so that scripts load last
questions.why: Why A is right: the deck states the head holds meta-information — title, character encoding, links to external resources — and "it is not visible to the user". Why the others are wrong: B describes `<body>` · C is false; the head is part of the document's required structure regardless of stylesheets · D inverts document order, a rationalisation from the real-world habit of putting scripts at the end of `<body>`.

questions.q: An external hyperlink must open in a new tab. Which line follows the deck's rules for external links?
options: `Miva`
`Miva`
`Miva`
`Miva`
questions.why: Why D is right: the deck requires external links to give the complete URL including the protocol, and names `target="_blank"` as the way to open in a new tab or window. Why the others are wrong: A omits the protocol, making the href a relative path, and invents an attribute · B uses `src`, which belongs on ``, not ``, and `_new` is not a standard target · C is an in-page fragment link, so it goes nowhere external.

questions.q: The deck's mid-lesson answer names three elements used for text formatting. They are:
options: `<strong>`, `<em>`, `<mark>`
questions.why: Why B is right: the mid-lesson answer names `<strong>`, `<em>` and `<u>` with the purposes "strong importance", "emphasise" and "underline for visual emphasis". Why the others are wrong: A gives the presentational pair `<b>` and `<i>`, which is what a developer would name first and is not the deck's answer · C swaps `<u>` for `<mark>`, which the deck never mentions · D lists structural elements, not formatting ones.

questions.q: The deck distinguishes the `name` and `id` attributes on a form input as follows:
options: `name` identifies the element in the page; `id` is submitted to the server
both are submitted, and `id` is used only when `name` is absent
`name` is submitted with the form data; `id` uniquely identifies the element
`name` is required by HTML5 validation; `id` is required by the `action` attribute
questions.why: Why C is right: the deck states both roles — `name` is used when submitting form data; `id` is a unique identifier used with labels and scripting. Why the others are wrong: A reverses them, which is the whole point of the question · B invents a fallback rule that does not exist · D attaches `name` to validation and `id` to the `action` attribute, neither of which is true.

questions.q:
Consider the following form.
```html
<form action="/upload.php" method="post">
  <input type="file" name="cv">
  <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>
```
The uploaded file never reaches the server script. Which named attribute is missing?
options: `accept="*/*"` on the `<input>` element
`multiple` on the `<input>` element
`method="get"` in place of `method="post"`
`enctype="multipart/form-data"` on the `<form>` element
questions.why: Why D is right: the deck names it explicitly — `enctype="multipart/form-data"` is necessary on the form when handling file uploads on the server. Why the others are wrong: A only filters the file picker's dialogue and affects nothing on the server · B allows several files, but none of them would arrive either · C makes it worse: a GET form cannot carry a file body at all.

questions.q: The difference between GET and POST, as the deck presents it for forms, is that:
options: GET appends data to the URL as query parameters; POST sends it in the request body
GET encrypts the data in transit, while POST leaves it readable
GET creates new records on the server; POST retrieves existing ones
GET can carry uploaded files; POST is restricted to plain text
questions.why: Why A is right: the deck says GET appends form data to the URL as query parameters and POST sends it in the request body. Why the others are wrong: B is the course's own error restated — the Week 3 deck claims POST sends data "securely", but POST is not encrypted; only HTTPS encrypts · C describes the REST/CRUD mapping of POST and GET in Week 2, and reverses it besides · D is false; POST is not restricted to text and GET cannot carry a body of files.

questions.q:
Consider the following input.
```html
<input type="text" name="zip" pattern="[0-9]{5}" required>
```
What does the `pattern` attribute enforce here?
options: a value of at most five characters of any kind
a value of exactly five digits
any number between 0 and 9999
five characters of which at least one is a digit
questions.why: Why B is right: `[0-9]{5}` matches exactly five digit characters; the deck's own words are that the pattern "ensures that the input value is a 5-digit number". Why the others are wrong: A describes `maxlength="5"`, a different attribute · C would accept "42", which has fewer than five digits · D would be a much looser pattern; `{5}` fixes the count and `[0-9]` fixes the character class, so every one of the five must be a digit. --- ### Week 4 — CSS selectors, the box model, layout and typography

questions.q: The deck's definition of CSS emphasises that it:
options: replaces HTML tags with styling rules at render time
converts an HTML document into a tree of styled nodes
compiles styling rules into JavaScript when the page loads
separates the content (HTML) from its presentation (styling)
questions.why: Why D is right: the deck's definition ends "CSS separates the content (HTML) from its presentation (styling)" — the sentence to open any CSS answer with. Why the others are wrong: A has CSS replacing markup rather than styling it · B describes the DOM, a Week 7 topic · C invents a compilation step that does not exist.

options: class, ID, universal
type, class, descendant
ID, class, descendant
ID, type, universal
questions.why: Why C is right: `#header` is an **ID** selector, `.button` a **class** selector, and `article p` a **descendant** selector. Why the others are wrong: A reverses the first two, which is the error of reading `#` as "class" · B calls `#header` a type selector — type selectors take a bare tag name, like `p` · D calls `.button` a type selector and `article p` universal; the universal selector is `*`.

questions.q: The four components of the CSS box model, from innermost outwards, are:
options: content, padding, border, margin
content, border, padding, margin
margin, border, padding, content
padding, content, border, margin
questions.why: Why A is right: the deck names four components and works inward-out: content, padding, border, margin. Why the others are wrong: B swaps padding and border — padding sits *inside* the border, not outside it · C runs the list backwards, outermost first · D puts padding inside the content box, which reverses their relationship.

questions.q:
Consider the following rule.
```css
.Following the deck's own arithmetic, what is the total width of this element when content, padding, border and margin are all added together?
options: 244px
224px
264px
200px
questions.why: Why C is right: the deck's arithmetic is 200 (content) + 40 (left and right padding) + 4 (left and right border) + 20 (left and right margin) = **264px**. Why the others are wrong: A stops at content + padding + border and forgets the margin · B counts padding and margin but drops the border · D is the declared `width` alone, which is what you get if you assume `box-sizing: border-box` — a habit from real work, and `box-sizing` appears nowhere in this course.

questions.q: The deck describes CSS Grid Layout, and only CSS Grid Layout, as:
options: a one-dimensional model distributing space along a single axis
a two-dimensional grid system giving control over rows and columns
a technique for floating elements left or right within a container
a way of setting elements to `inline-block` so they sit side by side
questions.why: Why B is right: the deck calls Grid "a two-dimensional grid system enabling precise control over rows and columns", and says this of Grid only. Why the others are wrong: A describes Flexbox, which is the discriminator being tested · C describes `float` · D describes `display: inline-block`. All three are real layout techniques from the same lesson.

questions.q: In Flexbox, `justify-content` and `align-items` operate as follows:
options: `justify-content` on the main axis; `align-items` on the cross axis
`justify-content` on the cross axis; `align-items` on the main axis
both act on the main axis, in opposite directions
`justify-content` is always horizontal; `align-items` is always vertical
questions.why: Why A is right: `justify-content` distributes along the **main** axis; `align-items` aligns along the **cross** axis. Why the others are wrong: B reverses them, the most frequent Flexbox error · C collapses the distinction into one axis · D is true only while `flex-direction: row`; set `column` and both axes rotate, which is exactly why the deck defines them by axis and not by direction.

questions.q: The default value of `align-items` is:
options: `flex-start`
`center`
`baseline`
`stretch`
questions.why: Why D is right: the deck lists `align-items` values as flex-start, flex-end, center, baseline and **stretch, the default**. Why the others are wrong: A is the default for `justify-content`, not `align-items`, and is what most students guess · B and C are valid values but not the default.

questions.q: The `flex` shorthand accepts its three values in this order:
options: flex-basis, flex-grow, flex-shrink
flex-grow, flex-shrink, flex-basis
flex-shrink, flex-grow, flex-basis
flex-grow, flex-basis, flex-shrink
questions.why: Why B is right: the deck states the shorthand accepts "flex-grow, flex-shrink, and flex-basis in that order". Why the others are wrong: A, C and D are the three plausible permutations. Grow before shrink before basis is the only order the deck gives, and it is a straight recall mark. --- ### Week 5 — JavaScript fundamentals

questions.q: According to the Week 5 material, JavaScript:
options: was developed by Douglas Crockford and runs only on the server
was developed by Brendan Eich as a server-side alternative to PHP
was developed by Brendan Eich and is a client-side scripting language
is a markup language, like HTML, used to describe page structure
questions.why: Why C is right: the Week 5 Summary names **Brendan Eich** as JavaScript's developer and calls it a client-side scripting language running in the user's browser rather than on the server. Why the others are wrong: A names the author of *JavaScript: The Good Parts*, which is the course's key reference for this week — a genuinely tempting swap · B has the right person and the wrong side of the network · D contradicts the deck's insistence that "unlike HTML and CSS, JavaScript is a full-fledged programming language".

questions.q: The deck's stated rule for `let` and `const` is that:
options: `let` variables can be reassigned, while `const` variables are read-only
both may be reassigned, but `const` may not be redeclared
`const` variables are immutable, so their contents can never change
`let` is function-scoped while `const` is block-scoped
questions.why: Why A is right: the deck's rule is that variables declared with `let` can be reassigned, while those declared with `const` are **read-only**. Why the others are wrong: B invents a redeclaration rule · C overstates it: `const` prevents reassignment of the binding, not mutation of the object it holds — claiming immutability says more than the course does and more than is true · D reverses the scoping; `var` is the function-scoped keyword, and block scope arrived *with* `let` and `const` together.

options: false then false
false then true
true then false
true then true
questions.why: Why C is right: `==` compares values after type coercion, so `5 == "5"` is true; `===` is the **strict** operator and also checks the data type, so `5 === "5"` is false. Why the others are wrong: A treats `==` as strict too · B reverses both results · D is the answer of someone who knows the two operators differ but not which is the loose one.

questions.q: Of the five array methods named in the deck, which is described as creating a new array?
options: `push()`
`pop()`
`splice()`
`filter()`
questions.why: Why D is right: the deck says `filter()` "creates a new array with all elements that pass a test", and says "creates a new array" of no other method. Why the others are wrong: A appends to the end of the original array · B removes the last element from the original · C adds, removes or replaces at an index — all three mutate in place. The distinction between mutating and non-mutating methods is what this question tests.

Why B is right: 8 × 4 = **32**, and the deck states this result explicitly in its mid-lesson answer. Why the others are wrong: A is 8 + 4, from misreading `*` as `+` · C is 8 × 3 · D is the two arguments concatenated as strings, which is what would happen with `length + width` if either were a string.

questions.q: The three types of variable scope named in the JavaScript lesson are:
options: global, local and static
public, private and protected
lexical, dynamic and global
global, local and block
questions.why: Why D is right: the JavaScript lesson names **global, local and block** scope, and says block scope was "introduced in modern JavaScript with `let` and `const`". Why the others are wrong: A is the **PHP** answer from Week 9 — static is PHP's third scope and JavaScript has no equivalent in this course; mixing the two lists is the trap · B lists access modifiers from class-based languages · C names two real concepts that the course never uses.

questions.q: A closure is defined in the deck as a feature that allows a function to:
options: keep access to variables from its enclosing function after that function has returned
run immediately after it is created, without being called explicitly
bind `this` to the context of the function that encloses it
be passed as an argument to another function and executed later
questions.why: Why A is right: the deck defines a closure as a function that maintains access to variables from its enclosing function "even after the outer function has finished executing". Why the others are wrong: B defines an IIFE · C describes what an arrow function does with `this` · D describes a callback. All three appear on nearby slides in the same lesson.

questions.q: An IIFE is used principally to:
options: delay execution until the event loop is idle
bind `this` lexically inside an event handler
create a private scope and keep variables out of the global scope
let a function call itself until a base case is reached
questions.why: Why C is right: the deck says an IIFE creates "a private scope for variables and prevent[s] them from polluting the global scope", and helps avoid name collisions in large projects. Why the others are wrong: A describes `setTimeout` scheduling · B describes arrow functions' lexical `this` · D describes recursion. Note the IIFE's *immediate* execution is its mechanism; the private scope is its stated purpose. --- ### Week 6 — Asynchronous JavaScript, ES6, AJAX and events

questions.q: The deck presents three approaches to asynchronous programming, in this order:
options: promises, callbacks, async/await
callbacks, promises, async/await
async/await, promises, callbacks
callbacks, generators, promises
questions.why: Why B is right: the deck presents callbacks first as "a fundamental way of handling asynchronous operations", then promises as "a more structured way", then async/await as "more modern and concise". Why the others are wrong: A and C invert the historical and pedagogical order the deck uses · D substitutes generators, which the course never names.

questions.q: ES6 is also known as:
options: ECMAScript 2015, the sixth major version of the specification
ECMAScript 2016, the sixth major version of the specification
ECMAScript 6.0, the sixth release of JavaScript by Netscape
ECMAScript 2015, the sixth release of the Node.js runtime
questions.why: Why A is right: the deck says ES6 "also known as ECMAScript 2015, is the sixth major version of the ECMAScript language specification". Both the year and "sixth" are examinable. Why the others are wrong: B gives 2016, which is ES7 · C attributes the specification to Netscape, confusing JavaScript's origin with ECMAScript's standardisation · D confuses the language specification with the Node.js runtime, which versions independently.

options: destructuring
the spread operator
arrow functions
template literals
questions.why: Why D is right: backticks with `${}` interpolation are **template literals**, which the deck describes as giving multi-line strings and embedded expressions. Why the others are wrong: A extracts values out of arrays and objects · B copies or gathers with `...` · C is the shorter function syntax that binds `this` lexically. All four are on the deck's seven-feature ES6 list, which is why identifying the right one matters.

questions.q: AJAX stands for:
options: Automatic JavaScript and XHTML
Asynchronous Java and XML
Asynchronous JavaScript and XML
Asynchronous JavaScript and JSON
questions.why: Why C is right: AJAX is **Asynchronous JavaScript and XML**. Why the others are wrong: A and B corrupt one word each — "Automatic" for "Asynchronous", "Java" for "JavaScript"; Java and JavaScript are unrelated languages · D substitutes JSON, which is the format AJAX almost always carries in practice and is not what the acronym says. Expand it as XML, then add that JSON is the common format — the deck says so itself.

questions.q: The deck contrasts `XMLHttpRequest` with the Fetch API. The stated advantage of Fetch is that:
options: it is not restricted by the same-origin policy
it returns promises, giving a more concise and readable syntax
it sends data without making an HTTP request at all
it parses JSON automatically, with no further call needed
questions.why: Why B is right: the deck describes Fetch as "a modern alternative... it returns promises for a more concise and readable syntax". Why the others are wrong: A is false — Fetch is bound by the same-origin policy exactly as XMLHttpRequest is, and needs CORS to cross origins · C describes no real mechanism · D is a half-truth turned into a falsehood: `response.json()` is still an explicit call, and it returns a promise of its own.

questions.q: The same-origin policy and CORS relate to each other as follows:
options: the same-origin policy is the restriction; CORS is the mechanism that relaxes it
CORS is the restriction; the same-origin policy is the mechanism that relaxes it
both are restrictions, one applied by the browser and one by the server
CORS replaced the same-origin policy in modern browsers
questions.why: Why A is right: the deck names the same-origin policy as the restriction that limits requests to the same domain, and CORS as what you handle to make cross-domain requests possible. Why the others are wrong: B swaps restriction and relaxation, the standard confusion between the two names · C makes CORS a second restriction · D claims a replacement that never happened — the same-origin policy is still the default in every browser.

questions.q: The Week 6 material names four components of an event. They are:
options: event source, event target, event handler, event queue
event type, event listener, event bubble, event capture
event trigger, event type, event callback, event object
event source, event type, event listener, event object
questions.why: — **[no deck]** (events appear only on the Week 6 Summary; the deck covers async and ES6) Why D is right: the Summary names four components — event source, event type, event listener, event object. Why the others are wrong: A swaps in "target", "handler" and "queue", all plausible and none on the list · B replaces two components with propagation *phases* · C keeps the event object but renames the source and listener. The **event object** is the component students most often omit, so any option that keeps three and changes one is designed to catch a half-remembered list.

options: outer, then inner
inner, then outer
inner only
outer only
questions.why: — **[no deck]** Why B is right: `addEventListener` listens in the **bubbling** phase by default, so the event fires on the target first and then travels up: inner, then outer. Why the others are wrong: A is the capturing order, which you would only get by passing `true` as the third argument · C assumes propagation stops at the target, which is what `stopPropagation()` would do · D assumes the outer listener swallows the click. --- ### Week 7 — The Document Object Model

questions.q: The DOM is defined in the deck as:
options: a scripting language for manipulating HTML documents
a rendering engine that converts CSS into pixels on screen
a programming interface representing documents as a tree-like structure
a data format for exchanging structured documents between servers
questions.why: Why C is right: the deck defines the DOM as "a programming interface that represents web documents (HTML, XHTML, or XML) as a tree-like structure called the DOM tree". Why the others are wrong: A calls it a language; the DOM is an interface that JavaScript uses, not a language itself · B describes the rendering engine, a different part of the browser · D describes a serialisation format like XML or JSON.

questions.q: In ``, the deck classifies `src` and `alt` as:
options: element nodes
text nodes
document nodes
attribute nodes
questions.why:
Why D is right: the deck is explicit that attributes are nodes, and gives `src` and `alt` on an `` as its example of **attribute nodes**. Why the others are wrong: A is the `` tag itself · B is the text inside an element, such as "Hello, World!" in a `

` · C is not one of the three node types the deck names. Remember the sentence that resolves this: every element is a node, but not every node is an element.

questions.q: Which statement about the DOM selection methods is correct?
options: `querySelector()` returns the first matching element and takes a CSS selector
`querySelector()` returns every matching element, as `getElementById()` returns one
`getElementsByClassName()` takes a CSS selector and returns a single element
`querySelectorAll()` returns the first matching element, selected by tag name
questions.why: Why A is right: `querySelector()` returns the **first** matching element and takes a **CSS selector**. Why the others are wrong: B gives `querySelectorAll()`'s behaviour to `querySelector()` · C confuses `getElementsByClassName()`, which takes a bare class name and returns a collection · D combines two errors — `querySelectorAll()` returns all matches, and it takes a CSS selector rather than a tag name.

options: `addEventListener` cannot be called on a `<button>` element
the handler must be given as a string rather than a function reference
`getElementById` expects a bare id, not a CSS selector, so `btn` is null
the element must be selected after the listener has been attached
questions.why: Why C is right: `getElementById` takes a bare id string. Passing `"#submitBtn"` matches nothing, `btn` is null, and calling `addEventListener` on null throws. Why the others are wrong: A is false; buttons take listeners normally · B describes the obsolete inline-attribute style, which is not what breaks here · D invents an ordering rule. The `#` prefix belongs to `querySelector`, and mixing the two APIs is the exact slip being tested.

options: Both lines render the tag as markup, so both are equally unsafe
`innerHTML` parses the value as markup and may run injected code; `textContent` does not
Neither line renders markup, because the value is a string
`textContent` parses the value as markup, while `innerHTML` escapes it
questions.why: Why B is right: assigning to `innerHTML` parses the string as markup, so the `onerror` handler in the injected `` runs — the XSS vector the deck warns about twice without explaining. `textContent` writes the string as text and renders nothing. Why the others are wrong: A treats both as unsafe, which loses the whole distinction · C assumes a string is inert regardless of how it is assigned · D reverses the two properties.

questions.q: Custom data attributes on an element are, according to the deck, prefixed with:
options: `attr-`
`custom-`
`data-`
questions.why: Why D is right: the deck says custom data attributes are "prefixed with `data-`". Why the others are wrong: A is the convention in Vue and Alpine templates, not the HTML standard · B and C are invented prefixes that read plausibly. --- ### Week 8 — Libraries and frameworks

questions.q: The Week 8 material distinguishes libraries from frameworks as follows:
options: libraries hold pre-written code for specific tasks; frameworks dictate the overall structure
libraries dictate the overall structure; frameworks hold code for specific tasks
libraries run in the browser, while frameworks run on the server
libraries are compiled ahead of time, while frameworks are interpreted
questions.why: Why A is right: the Week 8 Summary's discriminator is that "libraries consist of pre-written code for specific tasks, while frameworks dictate the overall application structure". Why the others are wrong: B reverses it, which is the mark being tested · C splits them by client and server, but jQuery and Express are on the same side of that line as their opposites · D splits them by compilation, which is unrelated to either definition.

questions.q: Which set are the five features of jQuery named in the deck?
options: DOM manipulation, routing, state management, animation, templating
utility functions, chaining, performance optimisation, animation, AJAX
DOM manipulation, event handling, AJAX requests, animation, cross-browser compatibility
date parsing, event handling, AJAX requests, animation, locale support
questions.why: Why C is right: the deck gives jQuery five features on five slides — DOM manipulation, event handling, AJAX requests, animation, cross-browser compatibility. Why the others are wrong: A substitutes concerns from modern frameworks (routing, state management, templating) · B is **Lodash's** feature list with animation and AJAX added · D opens with Moment.js's date parsing and closes with its locale support.

questions.q: Lodash and Moment.js are described in the deck as, respectively:
options: Lodash a date library, and Moment.js a utility library for arrays and objects
Lodash a utility library for arrays, objects and strings, and Moment.js a date library
two utility libraries, one intended for the client and one for the server
Lodash a DOM manipulation library, and Moment.js a testing library
questions.why: Why B is right: Lodash is "a modern JavaScript utility library... for arrays, objects, strings"; Moment.js is "a library for parsing, formatting, and manipulating dates and times". Why the others are wrong: A swaps the two libraries' purposes · C erases the distinction entirely · D gives Lodash jQuery's job and invents a testing role for Moment.js.

questions.q: React's virtual DOM is described as working by:
options: comparing the virtual DOM with the real DOM and updating only the necessary parts
re-rendering every component from scratch whenever any state changes
keeping a copy of the DOM on the server and syncing it over WebSocket
binding the UI to the data model so a change in one alters the other
questions.why: Why A is right: the deck says React "tracks the difference between the virtual DOM and the actual DOM and updates only the necessary parts". Why the others are wrong: B describes what the virtual DOM exists to avoid · C invents a server-synchronised DOM · D describes **two-way data binding**, which is Angular's concept — React's stated concept is unidirectional data flow. Factual footnote: React actually diffs the new virtual DOM tree against the previous virtual DOM tree and commits only the resulting minimal patch to the real DOM; it does not read the real DOM to compare. The deck's phrasing is quoted here because the exam is set from the deck.

questions.q: Which pairing of framework and key concept matches the deck?
options: Angular — incrementally adoptable
Vue.js — dependency injection
React — two-way data binding
Angular — two-way data binding
questions.why: Why D is right: the deck names Angular's key concepts as modules and components, dependency injection, and **two-way data binding**. Why the others are wrong: A gives Angular Vue.js's defining property, "incrementally adoptable" · B gives Vue.js Angular's dependency injection · C gives React two-way binding, when React's flow is explicitly unidirectional. Every distractor moves one concept one framework sideways.

questions.q: Which pairing of backend framework and language is correct?
options: Django — Ruby; Ruby on Rails — Python
Django — Python; ASP.NET — C#
Express.js — C#; ASP.NET — JavaScript
Ruby on Rails — JavaScript; Express.js — Ruby
questions.why: Why B is right: Django is Python and ASP.NET is C#. The full mapping is Django/Python, Express.js/JavaScript on Node.js, Ruby on Rails/Ruby, ASP.NET/C#. Why the others are wrong: A swaps Django and Rails · C swaps Express.js and ASP.NET · D swaps Rails and Express.js. Each is one transposition away from correct.

options: The route handler runs first, and `requireLogin` then cancels the response
Neither middleware runs, since `app.use` applies only to POST requests
The logger runs, then `requireLogin` sends a 401 and the route handler never runs
The logger runs, `requireLogin` runs, and the dashboard is sent with a 401 status
questions.why: Why C is right: middleware runs in the order it is declared. The logger registered with `app.use` runs first, then `requireLogin` finds no session user, returns a 401 and never calls `next()`, so the route handler is never reached. Why the others are wrong: A reverses the order, ignoring that `requireLogin` is listed before the handler · B is false — `app.use` applies to every method, not only POST · D has both the 401 and the dashboard body being sent, which cannot happen: `requireLogin` returns before calling `next()`. --- ### Week 9 — PHP

questions.q: PHP stands for Hypertext Preprocessor and is described as:
options: a client-side scripting language interpreted by the browser
a markup language for structuring dynamic web content
a compiled language that runs inside the web server's binary
a server-side scripting language whose output reaches the browser as HTML
questions.why: Why D is right: the deck calls PHP "a widely-used server-side scripting language"; the week's topic is embedding it in HTML, and the browser receives only the resulting HTML. Why the others are wrong: A makes PHP client-side, confusing it with JavaScript — the browser never sees PHP at all · B calls it a markup language, though the expansion "Hypertext Preprocessor" encourages that mistake · C claims compilation, which the deck does not.

questions.q: Which set of data types does the PHP lesson name?
options: String, Integer, Float, Boolean, Array, Object, NULL
String, Number, Boolean, Array, Object, NULL, Undefined
String, Integer, Float, Boolean, Array, Object, Resource
String, Integer, Double, Boolean, List, Map, NULL
questions.why: Why A is right: the deck names seven — String, Integer, Float/Double, Boolean, Array, Object, NULL. Why the others are wrong: B is the **JavaScript** list with Undefined added, and collapses Integer and Float into "Number" · C swaps NULL for Resource, which is a real PHP type the deck does not list · D renames Array and Object as List and Map. PHP itself also has Resource and, in modern versions, callable and iterable; the lesson lists only these seven.

options: WebTechnologies, using the addition operator
Web Technologies, using the concatenation operator
Web + Technologies, using the concatenation operator
an error, because PHP joins strings with `+`
questions.why: Why B is right: PHP concatenates with the **dot** operator, so `$first . " " . $second` produces `Web Technologies` including the space. Why the others are wrong: A names the addition operator and drops the space · C prints the dot as though it were a literal `+` · D asserts PHP uses `+` for strings — that is JavaScript's operator, and this is the likeliest one-mark discriminator between the PHP and JavaScript questions on the paper.

questions.q: The three types of variable scope named in the PHP lesson are:
options: global, local and block
public, private and static
global, local and static
global, lexical and static
questions.why: Why C is right: the PHP lesson names **local, global and static**, with static variables described as retaining their values across function calls. Why the others are wrong: A is the **JavaScript** list from Week 5 — block scope belongs there, static belongs here · B lists class access modifiers · D substitutes "lexical", a JavaScript term the PHP lesson never uses.

options: 120, and it is the base case that stops the recursion
15, and it is the base case that stops the recursion
120, and it is the increment that advances the recursion
720, and it is the terminating condition of a loop
questions.why: Why A is right: 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = **120**, and the deck names `$n <= 1` explicitly as "the base case [that] defines when the recursion should stop". Why the others are wrong: B is 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1, the sum rather than the product · C has the right value but calls the base case an increment, inverting its role — it terminates rather than advances · D gives factorial(6) and calls the condition a loop terminator, when there is no loop here.

questions.q: The loop constructs available in PHP are:
options: for, while, repeat-until and foreach
for, forEach, while and do-while
for, while, do-while and for-in
for, while, do-while and foreach
questions.why: — **[no deck]** (the deck names "looping structures" and then covers no loops at all; the summary lists them) Why D is right: PHP's four loop constructs are `for`, `while`, `do-while` and `foreach`. Why the others are wrong: A substitutes repeat-until, which is Pascal · B substitutes `forEach`, a JavaScript array *method*, not a PHP construct — and drops `foreach` · C gives `for-in`, a JavaScript statement. `foreach` is the construct that distinguishes PHP's loops from JavaScript's, so any option missing it is wrong.

questions.q: The lesson distinguishes parameters from arguments as follows:
options: parameters are supplied at the call; arguments are declared in the definition
parameters must carry default values, while arguments must not
parameters are named when the function is defined; arguments are the values passed at the call
parameters are passed by reference, while arguments are passed by value
questions.why: Why C is right: the deck states it word for word — "when we define a function, we specify its parameters. When we call the function, we provide the actual values, called arguments." Why the others are wrong: A reverses the two terms, which is the whole question · B invents a rule about defaults; defaults are optional and sit on parameters · D describes a passing convention, which is a different distinction altogether. --- ### Week 10 — Backend programming, server environments, databases and APIs

questions.q: The mid-lesson answer recommends Node.js for a real-time stock price feed because of:
options: its compiled bytecode and static type system
its event-driven, non-blocking I/O model and many concurrent connections
its built-in object-relational mapping layer
its elegant syntax and convention-over-configuration defaults
questions.why: Why B is right: the deck's own mid-lesson answer names Node.js for real-time stock prices "due to its event-driven, non-blocking I/O model" and its ability to handle many concurrent connections. Why the others are wrong: A describes Java, which the deck praises for reliability and scalability instead · C describes Rails' Active Record, an ORM · D quotes the deck's phrases for Ruby ("elegant syntax") and Rails ("convention over configuration").

questions.q: LAMP stands for:
options: Linux, Apache, MongoDB, Python
Linux, Nginx, MySQL, PHP
Linux, Apache, MariaDB, Perl
Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP
questions.why: Why D is right: LAMP is **Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP** — the deck's named web-server environment stack. Why the others are wrong: A and C substitute a different database (MongoDB, MariaDB) and a different language (Python, Perl) — Perl is the historical alternative that makes the P ambiguous outside this course, but the deck says PHP · B swaps Apache for Nginx, which is a real web server named elsewhere in the same lesson but is not the A in LAMP.

questions.q: ACID stands for:
options: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
Availability, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
Atomicity, Concurrency, Integrity, Durability
Atomicity, Consistency, Indexing, Distribution
questions.why: Why A is right: **Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability**. Why the others are wrong: B replaces Atomicity with Availability, which is the single commonest ACID error and probably comes from confusing it with the CAP theorem · C replaces Isolation with Integrity and Consistency with Concurrency · D replaces the last two letters with database techniques from elsewhere in this lesson.

questions.q: In the deck's table of database systems, MongoDB and Redis are described as:
options: MongoDB a relational database with fixed schemas, and Redis a document store
MongoDB a schema-less document-oriented store, and Redis an in-memory key-value store
MongoDB an in-memory key-value store, and Redis a document-oriented NoSQL database
both relational databases, ACID-compliant, open-source and SQL-driven
questions.why: Why B is right: the deck's table calls MongoDB schema-less and document-oriented NoSQL, and Redis an in-memory NoSQL key-value store used for caching. Why the others are wrong: A calls MongoDB relational, which is the error the schema-less row exists to prevent · C swaps the two — the memorable pair is "MongoDB stores documents, Redis stores keys in memory" · D makes both relational, which would put them alongside MySQL, PostgreSQL and Oracle.

questions.q: Normalisation is defined in the deck as organising data to:
options: speed retrieval by building additional lookup structures
spread a database across several physical servers
minimise redundancy and improve data integrity
convert relational tables into document collections
questions.why: Why C is right: the deck defines normalisation as organising data to "minimise redundancy and improve data integrity". Why the others are wrong: A defines **indexing**, the adjacent term in the same eight-item glossary and the usual swap · B describes replication or horizontal scaling · D describes migrating to a document store, which is not a normalisation step at all.

questions.q: An API endpoint is defined in the deck as:
options: a specific URL or URI that represents a resource or service
the server machine on which the API is hosted
the response returned to the client when a request succeeds
the authentication token supplied with every API request
questions.why: Why A is right: the deck defines an endpoint as "a specific URL or URI that represents a resource or service". Note that URI, not just URL, is in the definition. Why the others are wrong: B is what "endpoint" means casually in ops conversation, and it is the mistake the deck's wording guards against — the endpoint is the address of a resource, not the machine · C describes the response · D describes the authentication token, listed as a separate key term.

questions.q: Rate limiting is described as a mechanism that:
options: verifies the identity of a client using API keys or tokens
caps the size of the response body an endpoint may return
queues incoming requests until the database can serve them
restricts the number of requests within a specified time frame
questions.why: Why D is right: rate limiting "restricts the number of requests within a specified time frame to prevent abuse and ensure fair usage". Why the others are wrong: A defines **authentication**, the key term immediately before it in the deck's list · B invents a payload cap · C describes queueing or backpressure, which is not what rate limiting does — over the limit, requests are refused, not held.

questions.q:
Consider the following endpoints.
```
GET    /users
POST   /users
PUT    /users/123
DELETE /users/123
```
Following the deck's REST illustration, these four lines correspond, in order, to:
options: create, read, update, delete
read, create, update, delete
read, update, create, delete
create, update, read, delete
questions.why: Why B is right: the deck's REST illustration is GET → retrieve, POST → create, PUT → update, DELETE → remove. In the order shown, that is read, create, update, delete. Why the others are wrong: A gives the CRUD acronym's own order and so reverses the first two — the trap for anyone reciting "create, read, update, delete" without reading the fragment · C and D shuffle create and update, the pair most often confused, since POST creates and PUT updates.

questions.q: The Week 10 material says HTTP's lack of memory between requests is addressed by:
options: holding one TCP connection open for the whole of a user's visit
placing the user's data in the URL query string on every request
cookies or session management technologies that maintain state across requests
issuing the client a fresh API key with each request it makes
questions.why: Why C is right: the Week 10 Summary names "cookies or session management technologies" as what maintains user sessions and state across requests, answering HTTP's statelessness. Why the others are wrong: A confuses connection persistence with application state; keep-alive reuses a TCP connection but carries no memory of who you are · B is a real historical technique but not the course's named mechanism, and it exposes state in logs and history · D confuses API authentication with session state. --- ### Week 11 — Web application security, deployment and scaling

questions.q: The deck distinguishes a vulnerability from a threat as follows:
options: a vulnerability is a potential danger; a threat is a weakness in the application
both are weaknesses, one internal to the code and one external to it
a vulnerability is an attack that succeeded; a threat is one that failed
a vulnerability is a weakness in the application; a threat is a potential danger or harm
questions.why: Why D is right: the deck defines a vulnerability as "a weakness in a web application's design, implementation, or configuration" and a threat as "a potential danger or harm to a web application's security". Why the others are wrong: A swaps the two definitions, which is the mark · B erases the distinction · C recasts both as attacks, when a threat need never have been acted on and a vulnerability need never have been exploited.

questions.q:
Consider the following line of PHP.
```php
$sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '$user' AND password = '$pass'";
```
The attacker submits `admin' OR 1=1--` as the username. Why does the login succeed?
options: `1=1` is always true and `--` comments out the rest, so the password test never runs
the single quote escapes the password field, so an empty password is accepted
`OR` makes the database return every row, and the application selects the last
PHP reads `--` as a decrement, reducing the stored user id to zero
questions.why: Why A is right: the input closes the username string and appends `OR 1=1`, which is always true, then `--` comments out the rest of the query — so the password comparison never executes and the first row is returned. Why the others are wrong: B has the mechanism backwards; nothing about an empty password is accepted, the check is removed entirely · C misattributes the effect to row selection rather than to the always-true predicate · D reads `--` as PHP's decrement operator, when it is being interpreted by the **database** as a SQL comment.

questions.q: The distinction the deck draws between XSS and CSRF is that:
options: XSS tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request; CSRF injects a script
XSS targets the database directly, while CSRF targets files on the server
XSS injects a script into pages others view; CSRF makes a logged-in browser send an unwanted request
XSS is a server-side attack, while CSRF is an attack at the network layer
questions.why: Why C is right: XSS puts untrusted code on your page so it runs in another user's browser; CSRF uses a trusted browser's existing credentials to send a request the user never intended. Why the others are wrong: A reverses the two, the commonest confusion in Week 11 · B assigns them to the database and file system, which describes SQL injection and path traversal instead · D calls XSS server-side, when the script executes in the victim's browser.

questions.q: Which pairing of vulnerability and defence follows the deck?
options: SQL injection — output encoding and Content Security Policy
XSS — output encoding and Content Security Policy
CSRF — parameterised queries in every database call
XSS — unique session tokens issued on each request
questions.why: Why B is right: the deck pairs XSS with output encoding and names Content Security Policy as a tool that helps mitigate it. Why the others are wrong: A gives SQL injection XSS's defence — SQLi is countered with input validation and parameterised queries · C gives CSRF SQLi's defence; CSRF is countered with session management and unique tokens · D gives XSS CSRF's defence. Learn the three pairs as fixed: SQLi → parameterised queries, XSS → output encoding/CSP, CSRF → unique tokens.

questions.q: A Web Application Firewall is described as:
options: a service that filters and monitors HTTP/HTTPS requests as a shield against attacks
a network firewall permitting traffic only on ports 80 and 443
a code-scanning tool that finds vulnerabilities before deployment
an encryption layer protecting data at rest inside the database
questions.why: Why A is right: the deck describes a WAF as filtering and monitoring HTTP/HTTPS requests, acting as "a shield" and an "additional layer of security", inspecting traffic for malicious patterns and blocking them before they reach the application. Why the others are wrong: B describes a conventional network firewall, which works at the port level and cannot see request contents · C describes static analysis or vulnerability scanning, listed separately under security testing · D describes encryption at rest, a database concern.

questions.q: A VPS differs from cloud hosting in that a VPS:
options: draws elastically on the whole of a provider's infrastructure
places several websites on one server, sharing its CPU and RAM
is always sited within the organisation's own premises
partitions one physical server into several virtual servers, each with its own OS
questions.why: Why D is right: the deck defines a VPS as partitioning a physical server into multiple virtual servers, each with its own operating system, resources and configuration — "a balance between control and cost". Why the others are wrong: A is cloud hosting, which draws on a provider's whole infrastructure and scales elastically · B is **shared hosting**, where sites share one server's CPU and RAM without separate operating systems — the neighbouring option in the same four-way comparison · C is on-premises hosting.

questions.q: Horizontal scaling is:
options: upgrading an existing server with more CPU cores, memory or storage
moving the database onto faster storage to shorten query times
adding more machines or instances to spread the workload, often by load balancing
caching frequently requested pages at the edge of the network
questions.why: Why C is right: horizontal scaling adds more machines or instances and distributes the workload, "often achieved by load balancing". Why the others are wrong: A is **vertical** scaling, the reversal students make most often — the rule is horizontal means more boxes, vertical means a bigger box · B is a form of vertical scaling dressed as storage tuning · D describes a CDN, a performance technique rather than a scaling axis. If a load balancer is mentioned, it is horizontal.

questions.q: The deck's distinguishing point about a CDN, as against caching in general, is that:
options: it stores cached data in memory rather than on disk
it caches only the dynamic content the application generates
it takes the place of the origin server once the cache is warm
it uses geographically distributed servers to deliver content closer to users
questions.why: Why D is right: the deck defines a CDN as "networks of geographically distributed servers that cache and deliver web content from locations closer to users", reducing latency. The distance-to-user point is what earns the mark. Why the others are wrong: A describes in-memory caching, e.g. Redis · B is backwards; CDNs primarily cache **static** assets · C overstates it — the origin server still holds the authoritative content and serves cache misses.

questions.q: The three key concepts of monitoring named in the deck are:
options: metrics, debugging and version control
error handling, debugging tools and version control
unit testing, integration testing and end-to-end testing
metrics, alerts and logging
questions.why: Why D is right: the deck names three key concepts of monitoring — metrics, alerts and logging — each with a definition and an example. Why the others are wrong: A and B are the **debugging** list (error handling, debugging tools, version control), with A blending the two — answering a monitoring question with debugging content is the named trap here · C lists the three testing levels from the continuous-integration slide. Monitoring is continuous and pre-emptive; debugging is reactive. --- ### Week 12 — Future trends, PWAs and accessibility

questions.q: WebAssembly is described as:
options: a binary instruction format for browsers, compiled from languages such as C++ or Rust
a JavaScript library that speeds up numerical work in the browser
a browser plugin that runs native applications outside the sandbox
a text-based bytecode intended to replace JavaScript entirely
questions.why: Why A is right: the deck calls WebAssembly "a binary instruction format designed for web browsers", compiled from other languages "like C++, Rust, or TypeScript" and executed directly by the browser. Why the others are wrong: B makes it a JavaScript library, when it is a compilation target and a distinct format · C claims it escapes the sandbox, when the deck names sandboxed execution as one of its three advantages · D calls it text-based and says it replaces JavaScript — it is binary, and the deck frames it as addressing JavaScript's performance limits, not superseding the language.

questions.q: In serverless architecture, Functions as a Service is described as:
options: a hosting plan in which the provider supplies one virtual machine per function
the core of serverless architecture, where code executes in response to events
a library of ready-made functions supplied by the cloud provider
a billing model charging a flat monthly fee for each deployed function
questions.why: Why B is right: the deck calls Functions as a Service "the core of serverless architecture, where code is executed in response to events". Why the others are wrong: A reintroduces per-function virtual machines, which is exactly what serverless removes from the developer's view · C confuses FaaS with a provider's SDK · D contradicts the deck's stated cost model, which is paying only for the compute actually used during execution.

questions.q: The two challenges of serverless architecture named in the mid-lesson answer are:
options: cold starts and manual scaling
vendor lock-in and higher fixed costs
cold starts and vendor lock-in
network latency and the absence of encryption
questions.why: Why C is right: the deck's mid-lesson answer names exactly two challenges — **cold starts** and **vendor lock-in**. Why the others are wrong: A attaches manual scaling to serverless, when automatic scaling is one of its four named benefits · B attaches higher fixed costs, when cost-efficiency is another named benefit · D invents two challenges from general cloud discussion.

questions.q: Supervised and unsupervised learning are distinguished by:
options: whether the training data is labelled or unlabelled
the number of layers in the neural network used
whether the model runs in the browser or on the server
whether the output is a classification or an image
questions.why: Why A is right: supervised learning trains on **labelled** data; unsupervised learning trains on **unlabelled** data to discover patterns or groupings. That one word is the whole distinction. Why the others are wrong: B distinguishes **deep learning**, defined by neural networks with many layers · C is a deployment question and applies to neither definition · D confuses the learning type with the task; supervised learning covers regression as well as classification.

questions.q: The Week 12 material names service workers as the technology that gives PWAs:
options: responsive layouts that adapt to screen size and orientation
installation to the home screen through a JSON manifest file
encrypted transport between the application and the server
offline access, cached resources for faster loading, and push notifications
questions.why: — **[no deck]** (PWAs appear only on the Week 12 Summary; the Week 12 deck never mentions them) Why D is right: the Summary says service workers "enable offline access, caching resources for faster loading times, and providing push notifications to re-engage users even when the app is not open". Why the others are wrong: A is delivered by **responsive design**, listed separately as a PWA characteristic · B is delivered by the web app manifest, which the course never names · C is HTTPS — a prerequisite for service workers, but not what they provide.

questions.q: Among the four accessibility principles, providing alternative text for images is the example given for which principle, and using semantic HTML for which?
options: Operable, then Understandable
Perceivable, then Understandable
Perceivable, then Robust
Robust, then Perceivable
questions.why: Why C is right: the deck's example for **Perceivable** is providing alternative text for images, and its example for **Robust** is using semantic HTML so the site works with current and future technologies. Why the others are wrong: A gives Operable's example (keyboard accessibility) and Understandable's (plain language) to the wrong prompts · B keeps Perceivable but pairs semantic HTML with Understandable · D reverses the two. The mnemonic is **POUR**: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.

questions.q: A11Y is:
options: the WCAG conformance level required of public sector websites
a numeronym for the word "accessibility"
the name of the European Web Accessibility Directive
an ARIA attribute that announces a region to screen readers
questions.why: Why B is right: the deck defines A11Y as "a numeronym for 'accessibility'" — the letter a, eleven letters, then y. Why the others are wrong: A refers to WCAG conformance levels A, AA and AAA, which this course never mentions — do not build an answer on them · C names one of the two laws in the regulatory-compliance challenge, alongside the ADA · D describes ARIA, which is likewise absent from this course and is the answer a working developer reaches for first.
